# Conclusion  {#sec-discussion-outlook}

## Summary
Returning to the three questions posed in the introduction: demand is highly concentrated
in space and time. Downtown (the Loop and Near North Side) accounts for over 40 % of pickups
and O'Hare for a further 21 %, while the daily cycle runs from near zero overnight to a peak
around 17:00 (@sec-data-analytics). Community areas are the spatial unit best suited for fleet
management, being complete, free of interpolation artefacts, and small enough (roughly three
square miles) to act on, whereas census tracts are too sparse and privacy-suppressed to trust.
At this resolution, demand can be predicted well from calendar, weather, and location alone:
the feed-forward neural network reaches an R² of 0.90-0.93 and, at the recommended
4-hour/community-area resolution, cuts the error of a naive historical-average baseline
by roughly 18 % (nMAE 0.25 against 0.31, @sec-demand-prediction). The additional complexity
of the deep learning approach is therefore justified, as unlike the SVR it can train on the
full multi-million-row dataset and stays stable at finer resolutions where the SVR degrades.
Lastly, home charging of an EV taxi can be optimized with reinforcement learning: a tabular
Monte Carlo agent cuts charging cost by about 50 % against a naive full-charge baseline while
keeping energy shortfalls to 0.14 % of episodes (@sec-rl).

## Discussion & Limitations
For the fleet operator, these results translate into concrete operational guidance.
The network's community-area, 4-hour forecasts are precise enough to steer vehicle
pre-positioning: supply should be concentrated at O'Hare and downtown, with active
rebalancing back from the airport given its pickup-heavy asymmetry, and buffered
ahead of the evening peak and around weekends and holidays, where the demand *level*
shifts but not its *geography*. On charging, the RL results support relying primarily
on private, home-based charging for the bulk of overnight and mid-day replenishment,
since it is the setting the agent was trained on and it is where the roughly 50 % cost
saving materializes, as the operator directly controls timing and can shift power to
the cheapest, lowest-power slots. Public charging remains sensible as a complement
rather than a substitute, for opportunistic top-ups near O'Hare and the periphery,
where trips are highest in fare but also highest in energy use, and as a buffer
against the state-of-charge uncertainty the agent already plans around.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. On the data side, the demand models
drop the exact year and date to avoid overfitting on a short, ongoing 2024-2026
window, so they cannot yet learn a multi-year trend such as rising trip volumes
in growing areas; capturing this would require adding the feature back deliberately
or retraining the model regularly as new data arrives. The point-of-interest features
are static snapshots that cannot reflect how the POI landscape changes over time,
a limitation we accept because static POIs still help the model relate similar areas
to one another. The census tract layer is constrained by Chicago's privacy suppression,
which strips tract information from low-frequency trips: more than half of all records
lack it, tract boundaries may have shifted within the observation window, and the
resulting demand figures for suppressed or dropped records are filled with zero,
which improves model fit but is a modelling convenience rather than ground truth.
Coordinates throughout are area centroids rather than exact GPS points, so no encoding
recovers true spatial precision beyond the community area or census tract. Model-side,
the SVR's quadratic scaling meant it never saw more than a 50,000-row sample, so part
of its gap to the network reflects data availability rather than architecture alone;
the network's own depth search, in turn, was run once on a baseline configuration rather
than per experiment, due to compute constraints. On the RL side, the agent was trained
on a single, fixed home-charging window with a stylised cost and demand distribution,
so it is not yet validated against fleet-scale coordination of many vehicles or real
time-of-use electricity tariffs.

## Future Work
Three directions would most improve the pilot's next iteration. First, moving the
SVR to a linearly-scaling method, such as a Nyström-approximated kernel or a
gradient-boosted tree like LightGBM, would let it train on the full dataset
and give a fairer benchmark against the network, while an independent architecture
search per neural network configuration would tighten that side of the comparison.
Second, enriching the feature set with a genuine time trend and dynamic POI data,
alongside external sources such as scheduled events (excluded here for incomplete
timestamps), public transit disruptions, and electricity price feeds, could sharpen
predictions and add supply-side context currently missing. Third, the smart charging
agent should be extended from a single vehicle to a fleet-level setting with shared
charging infrastructure, variable tariffs, and vehicle-specific battery and route
profiles, closing the loop between where vehicles are needed, per the demand forecasts
and hotspot geography identified here, and when they can most cheaply be recharged.

## Discussion & Limitations
- As the exact year and date are dropped the model can not learn a trend over the years, e.g. increasing number of trips in certain areas. To solve this, the model should either take these additional information into account in future or must be regulary retrained to ensure the most up to date values
- Static values for the POI are a limitation. They might already be included in the target variable but we decided to keep them, as they may help the model to correlate between similar census tracts/ community area
- Spatial Limitation for census tract: only has half of the data
- Census tract is missing in most of the records, therefore it gets filled by 0s which improve the prediction in this context
- Census tract might have changed
- Demand might not be accurate due to removing of records, especially for the census tracts
- Coordinates are centroids and not exact locations
